detail.scope: Commercial-sector electricity sales and average price by state, as reported to EIA. Data centers are billed mostly in the commercial class, so this is a proxy for their load, not a measurement of it.

sources.name: ERCOT
sources.scope: Large generators with a full interconnection study requested, from the monthly Generator Interconnection Status report for Texas. Includes projects from study through commissioning.

sources.name: NYISO
sources.scope: Projects in the New York interconnection queue as NYISO publishes them.

sources.name: MISO
sources.scope: Projects in the Midcontinent generator interconnection queue, all statuses as MISO publishes them.

sources.name: Southwest Power Pool
sources.scope: Generator interconnection requests across the south-central US, all statuses as SPP publishes them, withdrawn requests counted separately.

sources.name: CAISO
sources.scope: Active generator interconnection requests on the California ISO grid, from the public queue report. Completed and withdrawn projects are counted separately.

analysis.body:
The five grid operators whose public interconnection files were harvested as of September 1, 2026 — ERCOT, NYISO, MISO, SPP, and CAISO — each maintain their own queue under different rules and scope definitions, so their totals cannot be simply added together or treated as a unified national picture. Within those separate queues, ERCOT's Texas queue is the largest by megawatt volume at roughly 438,086 MW across 1,778 requests, followed by NYISO at about 319,095 MW across 1,414 requests, MISO at about 299,721 MW across 3,828 requests, SPP at about 198,716 MW across 1,075 requests, and CAISO at roughly 71,682 MW across 265 requests. These are planned generation and storage projects waiting to connect to the grid, not data center demand itself; a crowded queue means developers want to build, but many projects will be delayed, modified, or withdrawn before they ever generate a watt.

For readers focused on AI data centers, the fuel categories most relevant as load-following or on-site backup signals are natural gas and battery storage, because data center campuses increasingly require firm or fast-responding power that solar and wind alone cannot guarantee. On that basis, ERCOT's queue contains roughly 78,092 MW of gas and 159,820 MW of storage; SPP shows about 47,392 MW of gas and 52,913 MW of storage; MISO carries roughly 30,236 MW of gas and 68,429 MW of storage; CAISO shows about 916 MW of gas and 46,944 MW of storage; and NYISO's published breakdown places nearly all of its 319,095 MW in an "other" category with 27,879 MW of gas, making storage comparisons with other operators unreliable from this snapshot alone. The concentration of storage requests in Texas and California in particular tracks with where large-scale data center development has been most active, even though the queue data cannot confirm a direct causal link.

The EIA commercial electricity sales figures for June 2026 — reported separately and serving only as a proxy for data center load rather than a measurement of it — show Texas leading the listed states at roughly 15,754 million watt-hours of commercial sales at an average price of $8.66 per kilowatt-hour, while Virginia logged about 7,771 million watt-hours at $10.99, and California posted about 10,025 million watt-hours at the highest listed price of $27.33; these state-level commercial sales totals reflect all commercial customers, not data centers alone, and carry the same caveat that they are not directly comparable across sources with different scopes. The pairing of high commercial sales volumes in Texas and Virginia with the large gas and storage queue positions in ERCOT and adjacent regions is consistent with ongoing load growth, though consistency is not confirmation. The key development to watch is whether ERCOT's 159,820 MW of queued storage and 78,092 MW of queued gas advance through study milestones into construction commitments over the coming quarterly queue update cycles.
